newsitem.title: CANADA: AWP official touts port labor bill to senators.
newsitem.headline: AWP official touts port labor bill to senators.

text.p: Alberta Wheat Pool chief executive Gordon Cummings met with Canadian senators to encourage passage of a bill that may ensure the transit of grain from elevators to vessels during port strikes.

"Customers are saying we are becoming less reliable. In the last 10 years we've had 10 work stoppages, mostly at the ports. I met with some senators this morning on the labor bill," Cummings told delegates of the Canada Grain Council.

The proposed amendment to Canada's labor code would require striking port workers other than those in the Grainhandlers' Union to transfer grain, an Agriculture Canada official said. The amendment is scheduled for third and final reading before the House of Commons before going to the Senate, the final stage before becoming law.
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien is widely expected to call an election later this month for an early June vote.
"This bill would make it illegal for grain to be stopped.
"If the longshoremen or stevedores go on strike, grain would still get through under the bill," said Vern Greenshields, spokesman for Agriculture Minister, Ralph Goodale.

Vancouver's last port strike in March, 1995, forced vessels to turn away and source grain from the United States. The strike also caused a six-week backlog throughout Canada's grain handling and transportation system.

Canada's reliability as a supplier of grains and oilseeds to the world market came into question again recently as weather and equipment-related delays caused a backlog of vessels at Pacific ports since early January.
"Argentina, the United States and Europe have all done a whole lot better than us," Cummings said.
"The fact we're selling cash now, rather than credit like we did to Russia in the '70s, means our customers will demand more from us," he added.
Cummings added his voice to grain industry calls for a system of rewards and penalties for early and late grain shipments by Canada's railways.
Goodale on Tuesday reiterated his commitment to putting such legislation in place.
